25.etyen:

Cognate with German abdizieren (outdated), Danish abdicere and English abdicate.

1000217.etyen: From French -iste (“-ist, -istic”), from Latin -ista (“-ist; one who practises or believes”), from Ancient Greek -ιστής (-istḗs), alternative form of -τής (-tḗs), from Proto-Hellenic *-tās, probably from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ (forms nouns representing state of being).

1000473.etyen:
The female given name has several possible origins. It may be a short form of Aurora or Aurelia. It may also be an independent adoption of aura (“breeze, air”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, breath”), the source of the common noun aura. In Finnish and wider Nordic naming tradition, it may additionally be associated with the Aurajoki (“Aura River”) and the allegorical name derived from it.
Compare Finnish Aura, Swedish Aura, Danish Aura and Faroese Aura (“female given names”).

en.g: pingo; a usually conical mound of earth or other loose material with a core of ice, occurring in regions of permafrost

En pingo er en mer eller mindre konisk haug som opptrer i arktiske strøk med permafrost.
A pingo is a more or less conical mound occurring in Arctic regions with permafrost.

1001241.etyen:
Borrowed from Greenlandic pingu (“tussock, small hill, hillock”), from Proto-Inuit *piŋu (“mound, dune, hillock, swelling”), ultimately from Proto-Eskimo *pəŋu (“hill, swelling”). Cognate with Inuktitut pingu (“hummock, small hill”) and Yup'ik penguq (“hill, mound”).
The term was adopted internationally as a technical term for an ice-cored permafrost mound during the 20th century.

Så gikk presten Hilkias og Akikam og Akbor og Safan og Asaja til profetinnen Hulda.

1001497.etyen:
Ultimately from Biblical Hebrew חֻלְדָּה (“Huldah”), the name of the biblical prophetess mentioned in 2 Kings 22:14–20 and 2 Chronicles 34:22–28.
The Biblical Hebrew name is traditionally analysed as a feminine formation related to חֹלֶד (“weasel; small burrowing animal”), from the root ח־ל־ד, associated with digging or burrowing. The precise animal denoted by the Biblical Hebrew word is uncertain and has variously been identified as a weasel, marten or mole-like animal; hence the name is conventionally interpreted as “weasel”. An alternative etymology connects the name with חֶלֶד (“life span,

en.g: a female given name from Jan or from Johanna [in turn from Latin, in turn from Koine Greek, in turn from Biblical Hebrew], equivalent to English Jane, derived from Jan or contracted from Johanna

1001753.etyen:
Either a feminine derivative of Jan or a contracted form of Johanna. Both source names belong to the Johannes name family. Johanna continues Latin Iohanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα (Iōánna), the feminine form of Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew יְהוֹחָנָן (Yəhōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”).
Compare Danish Janna, Swedish Janna and Finnish Janna (“female given name”).

1004825.etyen:
